scenes.title: Read Movement Paths and Projectile Directions
lines: As Gauss moves, follow the starting position and the line he travels. Watching where the enemies stood and how they react afterward helps connect the effect to the movement path.

Next, watch the attack motion and the effect spreading across the floor. The direction the character faces is different from the space around him. A selection screen should make clear which of these a choice changes.
In Dante's developer demonstration, glowing projectiles travel toward the direction he aims. Follow the character's position, the direction of travel, and the visible target at the far end.

Calling both actions attacks does little to explain the difference. Show whether a choice changes the space crossed while moving or an effect sent in one direction, and players will know what action to test.

scenes.title: Connect an Effect's Origin to Its Target
lines: When Dante raises his arms or aims ahead, look for where the bright effect first appears. Finding the motion near his hands and body makes the direction of the following light easier to read.
For the projectile shots, watch the space between the caster and the target ahead. Beyond the color of the effect, trace where it begins, which direction it takes, and where it appears to arrive.
Another shot shows a round blue effect near the caster. Compare the forward line with the round shape remaining nearby. These shots ask viewers to inspect different spaces.
You can build that connection into your own preview. Instead of only swapping a tool icon, reveal the action's origin, the space it covers, and the target used to check its effect in sequence.

scenes.title: Observe Ground Effects and Height
lines: Look more closely at Jade creating an effect on the ground. Identify the acting character, the light on the floor, and the nearby enemies separately, then connect the changes occurring in that space.
Now the character is airborne and aims downward. Unlike the ground-level shot, there is a difference in height. Watch the character's position together with the targets visible below.
The higher view helps distinguish targets on the ground from the aiming direction. The motion alone does not demonstrate that a particular equipment setting increased height or damage.

The viewpoint matters when explaining a choice's outcome. Keep the spatial relationship players can actually check, such as reaching along the ground or aiming down from above, in both the preview and the test.

scenes.title: Watch Nearby Targets and Surrounding Space
lines: Yareli's rotating effect moves with the character. Watch the character at its center together with nearby targets, rather than only following the circle. Their relative positions change the space that appears reachable.
Movement can carry you past a target or around its side. To explain a surrounding effect, a static size diagram benefits from showing the relative positions during actual movement as well.
Watch Dante's round effect with the same approach. Distinguish its visible center from the targets ahead. Similar shapes do not establish identical ability functions or values.
These shots do not supply an answer about the best ability. They offer a way to show players interested in nearby space where to look and what action to test.

scenes.title: Compare Target Arrangements First
lines: When Dante aims toward the doorway, first inspect the door and the visible targets in front of it. Follow the bright effect's direction as well to read which space he is acting toward.
Aiming from another position changes the angle between caster and target. A target centered on screen is not necessarily directly in front of the character. Consider the camera's position too.

In your own selection system, the same candidate could be tested against different arrangements. Prepare situations matching the player's purpose, such as targets grouped nearby and a target farther away.

The demonstration illustrates these spatial relationships. Instead of ranking performance because an effect looks larger in another shot, decide which conditions your own comparison will hold constant.

scenes.title: Define a Purpose Before Browsing Options
lines: Before entering a selection screen, describe the action you want to try in one sentence. Watching Dante, you might distinguish aiming at a target ahead from inspecting space near the caster.
Watch the arm-raising cast and the forward projectile motion in turn. Imagining the action that will change gives you a starting point before memorizing every name and number.

Then inspect the targets ahead and the space nearby. These shots do not contain a complete before-and-after settings change, so they cannot establish that applying a particular setting altered the effect.

In your own game, show the changing action beside a purpose-based starting choice. Lead the selected candidate into a short test of that purpose while preserving a path back to compare the original choice.

scenes.title: Match a Test Task to Its Result
lines: As Jade approaches a fallen ally, the intended recipient of help is clear. Watching the approach and subsequent recovery together explains what this test is trying to complete.

An attack test asks you to observe something different. When Dante aims ahead and sends out an effect, follow the initial motion and the target in front. It need not use the support shot's completion criteria.

Use the two shots to separate your own test goals. Provide someone to help for a support choice, or a position to check when changing reach. Watching only how spectacular an effect looks can obscure the purpose.
After the test, carry what was checked back into the selection screen. Returning to a candidate while remembering the observed result helps the player decide which part to change next.

scenes.title: Distinguish Play Style from Appearance
lines: Connect the real action shots we have examined. Moving forward along a path and sending an effect toward a target suggest different actions a player might want to try.
An effect near the caster or aiming downward from above changes the positions to observe. These differences can help explain selection outcomes and test situations in your own game.

The color and appearance previews coming next ask another question. Alongside which targets to affect, they ask what look to create. Appearance alone should not determine judgments about those actions' performance.
Prepare both a test for understanding an action and a preview for checking a desired look. Distinguishing the two helps players know what will change. Now we can move on to personal expression.
